items.title: 6.3.4 Tangents and Normals to a Parabola (Condition of the tangency to Parabola)

source_refs.note: Book p. 186-187: 6.3.4 tangent via dy/dx, normal, condition of tangency c = a/m for y^2 = 4ax.

blocks.text: To find an equation of the tangent to a parabola, we first determine the slope of the tangent at the given point by calculating \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) from the equation of the parabola. Using the point-slope form of a line, the equation of the tangent can then be written.
Since the normal to a curve at a point is perpendicular to the tangent at that point, its equation can be obtained readily from the equation of the tangent.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Two ideas from earlier work are used together here.
Slope of the tangent at a point = value of \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) at that point (differentiation, Unit 2).
Perpendicular lines: \(m_{1}m_{2} = -1\), so slope of normal \(= -\frac{1}{\text{slope of tangent}}\) (Unit 5).
The same rule works for every curve; 6.3.5 applies it to \(y^{2} = 4ax\). Below, the book first answers a different question: when does a given line touch the parabola?

Let us consider the equation of a line
\[y = mx + c\ \text{...(1)}\]
and the parabola
\[y^{2} = 4ax\ \text{...(2)}\]
To find their points of intersection, we solve equations (1) and (2) simultaneously. Substituting the value of \(y\) from (1) into (2), we obtain:

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
The book prints the third line as \(m^{2}x^{2} + 2mcx - 4ax + c^{2} = 4ax\). After moving \(4ax\) to the left the right side is 0:
\[m^{2}x^{2} + 2mcx - 4ax + c^{2} = 0\]
The next line (3) is correct.
Line (1) is tangent to (3) if roofs of (3) are equal. This implies discriminant D, of (3) is zero.
book_errors: Line (1) is tangent to (3) if roofs of (3) are equal.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Read: "Line (1) is tangent to (2) if the roots of (3) are equal." The line touches the parabola (2); (3) is the quadratic equation, and its roots (not "roofs") are the \(x\)-coordinates of the common points.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why equal roots mean tangency: each root of (3) gives one common point of the line and the parabola.
\(D > 0\): two different roots, two common points; the line is a secant (cuts the curve).
\(D = 0\): one repeated root, the two points merge into one; the line is a tangent.
\(D < 0\): no real root; the line misses the curve.
(This holds when \(m \ne 0\). A horizontal line \(y = c\) meets the parabola in exactly one point but crosses it; it is never a tangent.)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Here the quadratic (3) is \(Ax^{2} + Bx + C = 0\) with \(A = m^{2}\), \(B = 2(mc - 2a)\), \(C = c^{2}\), and \(D = B^{2} - 4AC\). In \(4amc = 4a^{2}\) we divide by \(4a\) (allowed, since \(a \ne 0\)) to get \(mc = a\).
Thus, the required condition for the line \(y = mx + c\) to be a tangent to the parabola \(y^{2} = 4ax\) is \(c = \frac{a}{m}\).
Consequently, for any non-zero real number \(m\), the line \(y = mx + \frac{a}{m}\) is a tangent to the parabola \(y^{2} = 4ax\). Similarly, we can find condition of tangency for other parabolas

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Point of contact (our addition, used in Exercise 6.3 Q10). With \(c = \frac{a}{m}\) the repeated root of (3) is
\[x = -\dfrac{B}{2A} = \dfrac{2a - mc}{m^{2}} = \dfrac{a}{m^{2}}\]
and then \(y = mx + c = \frac{a}{m} + \frac{a}{m} = \frac{2a}{m}\). So the line touches at \(\left(\frac{a}{m^{2}}, \frac{2a}{m}\right)\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Our example. Find the tangent to \(y^{2} = 8x\) with slope 2.
Here \(4a = 8\), so \(a = 2\); \(m = 2\) gives \(c = \frac{a}{m} = 1\). Tangent: \(y = 2x + 1\).
Check: \((2x + 1)^{2} = 8x\) gives \(4x^{2} - 4x + 1 = 0\), i.e. \((2x - 1)^{2} = 0\): a repeated root \(x = \frac{1}{2}\), point of contact \(\left(\frac{1}{2}, 2\right) = \left(\frac{a}{m^{2}}, \frac{2a}{m}\right)\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Tangent at a point: slope \(= \frac{dy}{dx}\) at that point, then point-slope form.
2. Normal: perpendicular to the tangent, slope \(= -\frac{1}{\text{slope of tangent}}\).
3. A line meets a conic where the substituted quadratic has real roots; equal roots (\(D = 0\)) mean the line touches.
4. \(y = mx + c\) touches \(y^{2} = 4ax\) if and only if \(c = \frac{a}{m}\) (\(m \ne 0\)); point of contact \(\left(\frac{a}{m^{2}}, \frac{2a}{m}\right)\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Expanding \((mx + c)^{2}\) as \(m^{2}x^{2} + c^{2}\) and losing \(2mcx\).
2. Taking \(B = 2mc - 2a\) instead of \(2(mc - 2a) = 2mc - 4a\).
3. Using \(c = \frac{a}{m}\) for the other parabolas. It holds only for \(y^{2} = 4ax\); for another parabola repeat the substitution (see 6.3.5).
4. Using \(D = 0\) when \(m = 0\): a horizontal line is never a tangent to \(y^{2} = 4ax\).
